Effects of the Merger

Upon the terms and subject to the conditions of the Merger Agreement, if the Merger is completed, Merger Subsidiary will merge with and into Kraton, and Kraton will continue as the surviving corporation and as a wholly-owned subsidiary of Parent. As a result of the Merger, our common stock will no longer be publicly traded and will be delisted from the NYSE and price quotations in the public market will no longer be available for our common stock. In addition, our common stock will be deregistered under the Exchange Act, and we will no longer file periodic reports with the SEC. If the Merger is completed, you will not own any shares of the capital stock of the surviving corporation.

At the effective time of the Merger, each share of Kraton common stock issued and outstanding immediately prior to such time (other than excluded shares) will be converted into the right to receive $46.50 in cash, without interest and less any applicable withholding taxes. At the effective time of the Merger, any shares held by Kraton (or any subsidiary or Kraton) as treasury stock or owned by Parent, Intermediate Merger Subsidiary, Merger Subsidiary or by any other subsidiary of Parent or Intermediate Merger Subsidiary will be cancelled and will cease to exist and no payment will be made with respect to such shares, and any shares held by stockholders who are entitled to demand and have properly demanded appraisal rights with respect to such shares pursuant to, and in compliance in all respects with, the DGCL will have the rights provided by the applicable provisions of the DGCL.

Each share of common stock of Merger Subsidiary issued and outstanding immediately prior to the effective time of the Merger will be converted into and become one newly issued, fully paid and non-assessable share of common stock of the surviving corporation.

As a result of the Merger, the Options and Company RSUs that are outstanding immediately prior to the effective time of the Merger will be treated as follows:

Each Option having a per share exercise price less than the Merger Consideration will be cancelled in exchange for cash in an amount equal to (1) the total number of shares of Kraton common stock for which such Option is exercisable, multiplied by (2) the excess of the Merger Consideration over the per share exercise price of such Option. Parent will then cause the surviving corporation to pay such amount less any applicable withholding taxes to each holder of the applicable Option through its payroll or otherwise at or reasonably promptly after the effective time of the Merger (but in no event later than three business days after the effective time of the Merger).

 

30

Each Company RSU that is outstanding immediately prior to the effective time of the Merger will be cancelled and converted into the right to receive an amount in cash equal to (1) the number of shares of Kraton common stock subject to such Company RSU immediately prior to the effective time of the Merger (as to any such PSUs, with such number of shares equal to the total Company RSUs outstanding and based on the actual performance of Kraton as compared to the applicable performance benchmarks as of the effective time of the Merger), multiplied by (2) the Merger Consideration. Parent will then cause the surviving corporation to pay such amount less any applicable withholding taxes to each holder of the applicable Company RSUs through its payroll or otherwise at or reasonably promptly after the effective time of the Merger (but in no event later than three business days after the effective time of the Merger).

The Board will also adopt resolutions or take action by written consent in lieu of a meeting prior to the effective time of the Merger that provide for the transactions contemplated above and that provide that no holder of any Option or Company RSU will have the right to acquire any ownership interest in Kraton or the surviving corporation.

At the effective time of the Merger, the certificate of incorporation and the bylaws of Kraton will be amended in their entirety to be in the forms set forth as exhibits to the Merger Agreement until thereafter changed or amended as provided therein or by applicable law. In addition, as of the effective time of the Merger, the directors of Merger Subsidiary immediately prior to the effective time will become the directors of the surviving corporation until their successors have been duly elected and qualified or until their earlier death, resignation or removal in accordance with the bylaws of the surviving corporation. Unless otherwise determined by Parent prior to the effective time of the Merger, the officers of Kraton immediately prior to the effective time will be the initial officers of the surviving corporation until their successors have been duly elected and qualified or until their earlier death, resignation or removal.

Background of the Merger

The following chronology summarizes the key meetings and events that led to the signing of the Merger Agreement. The following chronology does not purport to catalogue every conversation among the Board, members of Kraton’s management or Kraton’s representatives and other parties.

The Board and senior management of Kraton regularly review and assess Kraton’s business, operations and financial performance, including Kraton’s capital allocation strategy and potential opportunities to maximize stockholder value through acquisitions, business combinations, and other strategic and financial transactions. At least once annually and otherwise at regularly scheduled meetings of the Board, in connection with the Board’s oversight of Kraton’s business strategy and evaluation of growth opportunities, Kraton’s senior management updates the Board on Kraton’s recent activities and reviews strategic opportunities and challenges for Kraton in light of current market conditions and trends, and the Board discusses and evaluates such information. Kraton’s management and the Board also engage in discussions from time to time with various industry participants, including strategic parties and financial sponsors, as well as financing sources, market participants and investment banking firms, regarding Kraton’s business, strategy and growth opportunities, including opportunities for collaboration, potential business combinations, divestitures, acquisitions and financing transactions.

In September, November and December 2020, the Board held four meetings in which it discussed Kraton’s strategy with Kraton’s senior management. Representatives of J.P. Morgan, Kraton’s financial advisor, also participated in these meetings, and representatives of Kraton’s consultant

 

31

Table of Contents

on strategic matters at the time attended the meetings held in November and December 2020. Representatives of J.P. Morgan were invited to participate in these meetings due to their prior and ongoing experience in advising Kraton on strategic and other financial advisory matters, and the Board’s belief that J.P. Morgan had extensive experience advising companies in the chemical and polymer industries, as well as significant experience providing strategic and financial advisory services. At these meetings the Board received and reviewed various materials, including those prepared by J.P. Morgan and its consultant on strategic matters.

During these meetings, the Board engaged in a wide-ranging review of Kraton’s strategy and the assumptions underlying the strategy and plan. In particular, the Board discussed sustainability and innovation as business drivers, the role of Kraton’s two operating segments (chemical and polymer) in Kraton’s strategy, volatility in the price of Kraton’s common stock, competitive pressures in the chemical and polymer segments, and potential pathways to achieve additional and consistent growth and scale in Kraton’s chemical and polymer segments. Kraton’s senior management discussed with the Board the fact that Kraton’s chemical and polymer segments were two relatively distinct businesses, as well as management’s belief that growth and consistent leadership in the chemical segment would require environmental and sustainability considerations to become a major factor that drove customers’ behavior with respect to Kraton’s chemical product offerings. In addition, Kraton’s senior management discussed its belief that acquisitions of other complementary polymer businesses would be required to generate additional and consistent growth and value in Kraton’s polymer segment.

Following discussion, the Board determined that Kraton should pursue a corporate development plan primarily focused on (i) expanding and / or enhancing the existing polymer business through potential merger and acquisition transactions involving the acquisition of, or combination with, other parties’ polymer businesses and / or (ii) the sale of Kraton’s crude sulfate turpentine (“CST”) business (which constitutes a portion of Kraton’s chemical segment). The Board authorized Kraton’s senior management and J.P. Morgan to pursue this corporate development plan and discuss potential transactions in furtherance of the plan with third parties. On December 14, 2020, the date on which the Board authorized Kraton to pursue the corporate development plan, the closing sale price of Kraton’s common stock on the NYSE was $26.25.

During late 2020 and early 2021, in furtherance of the corporate development plan, Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan engaged in discussions with representatives of Party A, a strategic party, and Party B, a strategic party, regarding the potential acquisition of Party A’s and Party B’s respective polymer businesses or alternative business combinations involving their and Kraton’s respective polymer businesses. Each of Party A and Party B informed Kraton that it was not interested in exploring a sale of its polymer business or an alternative form of business combination involving its and Kraton’s polymer businesses.

Also during this period and in furtherance of the development plan, Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan engaged in discussions with Party C, Party D, Party E, Party F, and Party G, each of which was a potential strategic acquirer, regarding the possible sale of Kraton’s CST business. Each of Party C, Party D, Party E, and Party G informed Kraton that they might be interested in acquiring Kraton’s CST business, subject to further diligence and analysis. Party F informed Kraton that it was not interested in acquiring Kraton’s CST business.

On May 20, 2021, the Board met with Kraton’s senior management to receive an update on Kraton’s business and the corporate development plan. Representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP, Kraton’s legal advisor, also participated in the meeting. Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan also reviewed with the Board the discussions

that had taken place with the parties with respect to the corporate development plan. Among other matters, Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan discussed with the Board the fact that Kraton had been unable to gain any momentum with respect to the corporate development plan, noting that Party A and Party B declined to pursue a sale of their respective polymer businesses or an alternative form of business combination involving Kraton’s polymer business, and Party C, Party D, Party E, and Party G stated that they might be interested in potentially acquiring Kraton’s CST business, subject to further diligence and analysis. Representatives of J.P. Morgan informed the Board that they expected to have further clarity with respect to the interest of Party C, Party D, Party E, and Party G, regarding Kraton’s CST business by the middle of June 2021.

Also during the meeting, representatives of J.P. Morgan discussed with the Board the current state of the M&A markets, as well as their illustrative preliminary financial perspectives with respect to Kraton. Kraton’s senior management also reviewed with the Board the September, November and December 2020 strategy reviews conducted by the Board, and the determination to pursue the corporate development plan following these reviews. After discussion, including discussion as to results and feedback regarding Kraton’s corporate development plan in the prior six-month period, the Board determined that it would be in the best interests of Kraton and its stockholders to explore the potential sale of all of Kraton, and instructed Kraton’s senior management and J.P. Morgan to prepare a list of potential acquirers that could be interested in acquiring Kraton as well as a timeline and process to pursue such a transaction to be reviewed by the Board the following week. The Board also informed Kraton’s senior management and J.P. Morgan that it would review any proposals submitted by Party C, Party D, Party E, and Party G regarding Kraton’s CST business in connection with any proposals Kraton received to acquire all of Kraton. On May 20, 2021, the closing sale price of Kraton’s common stock on the NYSE was $33.82.

On May 24, 2021, the Board met with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP. During the meeting, the Board reviewed a list prepared by Kraton’s senior management with input from representatives of J.P. Morgan of potential buyers that could be contacted in connection with a potential sale of all of Kraton. This list included potential strategic acquirers, potential financial acquirers, and potential financial acquirers with portfolio companies in the chemical and polymer industries, and it also included Party A, Party B’s parent company and Parent. The Board discussed each potential acquirer, the reason for its inclusion on the list, as well as additional potential acquirers that were not on the list that might also be interested in a potential acquisition of Kraton. Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan noted that they did not believe Party C, Party D, Party E, and Party G would be interested in acquiring all of Kraton because Kraton’s polymer segment and the non-CST portions of Kraton’s chemical segment did not align with the businesses and strategic priorities of those parties. Representatives of J.P. Morgan also discussed with the Board a potential two-phase transaction process, whereby potential acquirers would submit initial indications of interests based primarily on publicly available information during the third week of June 2021, with the potential acquirers that submitted indications of interest that ascribed the greatest value to Kraton invited to participate in the second round of the process. Representatives of King & Spalding LLP reviewed with the Board its fiduciary duties in connection with a proposed process and a potential transaction. After discussion, the Board directed Kraton’s senior management to work with J.P. Morgan to contact the 14 possible acquirers that were discussed at the meeting to explore their interest in a potential acquisition of Kraton or its segments, and to commence the first round of the process as discussed during the meeting. On May 24, 2021, the closing sale price of Kraton’s common stock on the NYSE was $34.33.

In these initial discussions with the parties, representatives of J.P. Morgan, acting at the direction of the Board, informed the parties that while a proposal to acquire all of Kraton would likely be preferable to the Board and Kraton, the Board was focused on maximizing stockholder value and would evaluate any proposal (including a potential stock-based transaction or separate sale of Kraton’s segments) that the Board determined was reasonably likely to achieve this objective.

On June 3, 2021, the Board met with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of King & Spalding LLP to further discuss in detail the Board’s fiduciary duties in connection with a proposed process and any potential transaction. Kraton’s senior management also updated the Board regarding the initial outreach to potential acquirers.

By late June 2021, Kraton had entered into confidentiality agreements with 10 parties (including the party that made the “inbound” inquiry), six of which parties were potential strategic acquirers and four of which were potential financial acquirers. All of these confidentiality agreements included customary standstill provisions designed to facilitate an orderly process and maximize value for Kraton’s stockholders. The confidentiality agreements also provided that these standstill provisions would lapse if and when Kraton announced that it entered into a definitive agreement with respect to the sale of Kraton. Five of the parties that had been contacted by representatives of J.P. Morgan or Kraton’s senior management stated that they were not interested in pursuing a potential transaction and declined to sign a confidentiality agreement.

During the month of June 2021, the potential acquirers of Kraton engaged in preliminary due diligence activities. As part of these activities, Kraton’s senior management participated in preliminary management meetings with nine of the parties that had entered into confidentiality agreements with Kraton (five of which were strategic acquirers and four of which were financial acquirers). At these meetings, Kraton’s senior management reviewed Kraton’s expected near-term financial performance and innovation-related projects with the parties. One party that executed a confidentiality agreement with Kraton was invited to, but declined to participate in, this preliminary management meeting and informed representatives of J.P. Morgan that it was no longer interested in pursuing a potential transaction. In addition, Kraton’s senior management also participated in preliminary management meetings with Party C, Party D, Party E, and Party G regarding the potential sale of Kraton’s CST business.

Also during the month of June 2021, J.P. Morgan, at the direction of the Board, circulated a process letter to each party that executed a confidentiality agreement that requested initial indications of interest be submitted by June 29, 2021. The process letter instructed these parties not to engage in discussions with any member of Kraton’s senior management regarding the role of Kraton’s senior management following the consummation of a potential transaction, and no such discussions occurred prior to the signing of the Merger Agreement.

On June 18, 2021, Party E informed Kraton that it was no longer interested in acquiring Kraton’s CST business.

On June 23, 2021, Party D informed Kraton that it was no longer interested in acquiring Kraton’s CST business.

By July 2, 2021, Kraton received four indications of interest as part of the first-round process that contemplated a potential acquisition of all of Kraton. The per share purchase prices proposed by these parties were as follows: Party A proposed $42.00 to $45.00, Party H, a financial acquirer, proposed $41.00 to $43.00, Parent proposed $41.00, and Party I, a financial acquirer, proposed $40.00. Party K also informed Kraton that it was only interested in acquiring Kraton’s chemical segment in a transaction that was consummated independently of any potential sale of Kraton’s polymer segment to a third party (i.e., Party K was not willing to consummate a “back to back” transaction whereby Party K acquired Kraton’s chemical segment and another party simultaneously acquired Kraton’s polymer segment). Morgan provided a final bid procedures letter to Party A, Party H, and Parent that requested these bidders to submit markups of a draft merger agreement by September 8, 2021, and final indications of interest by September 15, 2021.

On August 22, 2021, the non-management members of the Board met in executive session. At the meeting, the directors reviewed an illustrative preliminary financial analysis prepared by J.P. Morgan with input from Kraton’s senior management that summarized the value that could potentially be achieved if Kraton were to either sell its chemical and polymer segments in separate transactions, or sell one of those segments and continue to operate as a standalone public company with the remaining segment (which potential transactions are referred to in this proxy statement as a “Sum of the Parts Strategy”). This analysis was based in part upon the proposal that Kraton had received from Party K to acquire Kraton’s chemical segment. The Board discussed the benefits and considerations associated with a Sum of the Parts Strategy, including among other matters the high degree of complexity and execution risk, the potential for stranded costs at the remaining standalone company, the potential inability to realize full value for Kraton’s polymer business, longer sales process, capital structure implications and costs, and the risks and volatility Kraton would face as a standalone public company if it were to sell one of its segments while retaining the other segment. The Board also reviewed the quantitative impacts that would affect the potential value achievable in such a transaction, including tax leakage, potential trading multiples, stranded costs, and dis-synergies. Depending upon certain assumptions with respect to these variables, this analysis indicated that a Sum of the Parts Strategy could potentially result, in a best case scenario, in a per share value ranging from approximately $44.00 to $51.00 per share (based on the midpoints of the analysis). After discussion, the Board determined to further review a potential Sum of the Parts Strategy with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP at a meeting the following week.

On August 30, 2021, the Board met with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP. At the meeting, the Board further discussed the value that could potentially be achieved if Kraton were to pursue a Sum of the Parts Strategy. Representatives of J.P. Morgan and Kraton’s senior management discussed with the Board the preliminary financial analysis that the Board had previously reviewed at its August 22, 2021 meeting. Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP discussed with the Board the benefits and considerations associated with a Sum of the Parts Strategy, including among other matters the high degree of complexity and execution risk, the potential for stranded costs at the remaining standalone company, the potential inability to get full value for Kraton’s polymer business, tax leakage, longer sales process, capital structure implications and costs, and the risks and volatility Kraton would face as a standalone company if it were to sell one of its segments while retaining the other. Representatives of J.P. Morgan also noted that Party K’s proposal to acquire Kraton’s chemical segment was still subject to significant due diligence and the receipt of firm financing commitments, Party K was the only potential acquirer that had been contacted that had expressed interest in acquiring Kraton’s chemical segment, and the only other non-withdrawn proposal Kraton had received regarding its chemical

 

37

Table of Contents

segment was from Party C , which proposed acquiring Kraton’s CST business for $100 million. Representatives of King & Spalding LLP discussed the timing and structural complexities that would be associated with a Sum of the Parts Strategy.

Following this discussion, and after considering the information provided by Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP, the Board determined that it did not believe that a Sum of the Parts Strategy was likely to deliver greater value for Kraton’s stockholders on a risk adjusted or absolute basis as compared to what could be achieved in a sale of all of Kraton in one transaction. The Board also determined that, although a Sum of the Parts Strategy was not likely to deliver greater value for Kraton’s stockholders as compared to what could be achieved in a sale of all of Kraton in one transaction, it would continue to evaluate all potential strategic alternatives available to Kraton, and the Board therefore instructed J.P. Morgan to request an updated proposal from Party K regarding its possible acquisition of Kraton’s chemical segment.

On September 7, 2021, the Board met with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP. At the meeting, Kraton’s senior management reviewed Kraton’s estimated third quarter business performance, as well as management’s outlook for the remainder of the fiscal 2021 calendar year. The Board then again discussed the Sum of the Parts Strategy with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP. Representatives of J.P. Morgan informed the Board that Party K would likely deliver its updated proposal to acquire Kraton’s chemical segment later in the week. After discussion, the Board determined that, while it continued to believe that a Sum of the Parts Strategy was not likely to deliver greater value for Kraton’s stockholders as compared to what could be achieved in a sale of all of Kraton in one transaction, it would revisit the issue after receiving Party K’s updated proposal.

On September 8, 2021, Parent and Party A submitted their markups of the draft merger agreement. Parent’s markup deleted the “hell or high water” regulatory provisions included in the Company’s draft merger agreement, which would have required Parent to, among other things, take all actions necessary (including through asset divestitures) to obtain any necessary regulatory approvals. Parent also proposed a Company termination fee of 3.5% of the enterprise value of Kraton (as compared to 2% of Kraton’s equity value in Kraton’s draft merger agreement) if the merger agreement was terminated by the Company so it could accept a superior proposal or by Parent because the Board changed its recommendation to vote in favor of the proposed merger, or by either party in certain circumstances described in the section titled “The Merger Agreement—Termination Fee; Effect of Termination” below. In addition, while Parent agreed that financing would not be a condition to consummation of the merger, Parent proposed that it would not be required to commence the “marketing period” process to obtain its debt financing until all conditions to closing had been satisfied, and Parent would not be required to close the merger until 20 business days after the end of the marketing period. In addition, although Parent required debt financing to consummate the merger, if Parent were unable to obtain its debt financing, the Company’s sole recourse would be to seek a specific performance remedy or pursue a claim for damages.

On September 9, 2021, Party K submitted an updated indication of interest whereby it proposed to acquire Kraton’s chemical segment for a purchase price equal to 9.5x the adjusted EBITDA of Kraton’s chemical segment for the trailing 12 months ending September 2021, subject to further diligence on the updated year-to-date results and the sustainability of those results on a go-forward basis. Party K ascribed a purported enterprise value for the chemical segment of $1.25 billion to this proposal. Party K also stated that its proposal was subject to certain purchase

 

38

Table of Contents

price adjustments (including with respect to incremental costs associated with how a potential carve-out transaction might be effected), and that it had not yet held any discussions with potential sources of debt financing and had not entered into any arrangements to provide the required equity financing to fund its proposed transaction.

On September 15, 2021, Parent provided a revised proposal to acquire Kraton for $46.00 per share. Parent noted that it had completed substantially all due diligence.

On September 17, 2021, Party A provided a revised proposal to acquire Kraton for $40.50 per share. Party A also proposed an alternative transaction whereby it would acquire Kraton’s polymer segment for an enterprise value equal to $1.3 billion, subject to certain adjustments, with Kraton’s chemical business being simultaneously spun off to Kraton’s stockholders. Party A also noted that its proposal was subject to additional due diligence.

On September 18, 2021, the Board met with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP. Representatives of King & Spalding LLP reviewed with the Board its fiduciary duties in connection with a potential transaction. Also during the meeting, the Board reviewed the updated proposals submitted by Parent, Party A and Party K. As part of this discussion, the Board discussed the regulatory approvals that would be required to consummate the merger, Kraton’s ability to accept a superior proposal, and Kraton’s remedies if Parent were unable to obtain its debt financing, and the benefits and considerations associated with a break fee payable by Parent in the event of a debt financing failure. The Board also reviewed an updated illustrative preliminary financial analysis prepared by J.P. Morgan with respect to a Sum of the Parts Strategy. This updated analysis incorporated the revised proposals submitted by Party K with respect to its proposal to acquire Kraton’s chemical segment, and Party A with respect to its proposal to acquire Kraton’s polymer segment, and was otherwise consistent in all material respects with the analysis reviewed by the Board at its prior meetings. This updated analysis also indicated that a Sum of the Parts Strategy could result, in a best-case scenario, in a value equal to approximately $46.00 to $48.00 per share (based on the midpoints of the analysis). The Board discussed a Sum of the Parts Strategy with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP, and the benefits and risks associated with such a strategy (all of which were the same as what the Board discussed at its prior meetings) and again determined that a Sum of the Parts Strategy was not likely to deliver greater value for Kraton’s stockholders as compared to what could be achieved in a sale of all of Kraton in one transaction. After discussion, the Board instructed J.P. Morgan to request that Parent increase its proposal to $46.50 per share, and to also inform Party A that its proposal did not provide adequate value to Kraton and its stockholders. The Board also instructed J.P. Morgan to inform Parent that Kraton would expect a reverse break fee, payable upon a termination of the merger agreement following a debt financing failure.

On September 20, 2021, representatives of Parent informed representatives of J.P. Morgan that Parent would increase its purchase price to $46.50 per share, and that this proposal was its best and final offer. Following Parent’s confirmation that it would increase its purchase price, King & Spalding LLP provided a revised draft of the merger agreement to O’Melveny & Myers LLP, as counsel to Parent (“O’Melveny”), along with revisions to the draft Company disclosure letter and a revised draft of the debt commitment letter. The revised draft of the merger agreement included, among other items, a termination fee payable by Kraton equal to 3% of equity value, revisions to the financing related provisions, and the addition of a reverse termination fee of 7% of equity value that would be payable by Parent if Kraton terminated the merger agreement as a result of Parent’s failure to obtain its debt financing, or if the merger agreement was terminated due to the

failure to obtain regulatory approvals. Between September 20, 2021 and September 26, 2021, Kraton, Parent, King & Spalding LLP and O’Melveny negotiated the terms of the merger agreement, ultimately agreeing to a Company termination fee of $63 million (approximately 4% of equity value) if the Merger Agreement is terminated by the Company so it could accept a superior proposal, by Parent because the Board changed its recommendation to stockholders to vote in favor of the proposed merger or by either party in certain circumstances described in the section titled “The Merger Agreement—Termination Fee; Effect of Termination” below. In addition, the parties agreed to a reverse termination fee of $63 million if the Company terminated the Merger Agreement as a result of the failure of the Debt Financing being available to Parent.

On September 21, 2021, Party A submitted an updated proposal in which it proposed to acquire Kraton for $42.00 per share, with an “earnout” structure in which Kraton’s stockholders could receive additional consideration if Kraton’s chemical segment were sold for amounts greater than certain thresholds.

On September 23, 2021, the Board met with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP. During the meeting, representatives of J.P. Morgan discussed Party A’s proposal with the Board. As part of this discussion, the Board discussed the risks and contingencies associated with Party A’s proposal and the fact that Kraton’s stockholders would not share in all of the value received in connection with a sale of Kraton’s chemical segment under Party A’s proposed earnout structure. After discussion, the Board instructed J.P. Morgan to inform Party A that its proposal did not provide adequate value to Kraton and its stockholders.

On September 24, 2021, Party A submitted an updated proposal whereby it would acquire Kraton for $44.00 per share. Party A’s proposal also contemplated a revised earnout structure whereby, if Kraton entered into a binding agreement to sell its chemical business to a third party prior to the closing of a transaction with Party A , then Kraton’s stockholders would receive 50% of the incremental net proceeds above certain thresholds. Party A stated that this proposal was its best and final offer and that it remained subject to confirmatory due diligence.

On September 26, 2021, the Board met with Kraton’s senior management and representatives of J.P. Morgan and King & Spalding LLP. Representatives of King & Spalding LLP discussed with the Board their fiduciary duties in connection with a potential transaction. The Board reviewed the terms of Party A’s most recent proposal. After discussing the terms of Party A’s proposal, including the earnout, the complexity, timing and risks (including regulatory risks) associated with the proposal, the Board determined that Party A’s proposal was not reasonably likely to deliver greater value to Kraton’s stockholders relative to the proposal from Parent.

The Board then discussed the Merger Agreement. Representatives of King & Spading summarized the material terms of the Merger Agreement, including the Merger Consideration, the representations being made by the Company and Parent in the Merger Agreement, the termination provisions of the Merger Agreement, and the additional covenants, including the interim operating covenants, the requirements that the Company seek stockholder approval of the Merger, the limitations on the ability of the Company to seek alternative proposals but its ability to respond to such proposals and change its recommendation and terminate the Merger Agreement to accept a superior proposal if required by the Board’s fiduciary duties. Representatives of J.P. Morgan then reviewed its financial analyses of the Merger Consideration contemplated by the Merger Agreement and rendered an oral opinion to the Board, which was confirmed by delivery of a written opinion, dated September 27, 2021, to the effect that, as of such date and based upon and subject to the assumptions made, procedures followed, matters considered, and limitations

on the review undertaken by J.P. Morgan in preparing its opinion, the Merger Consideration to be paid to the holders of Kraton common stock in the Merger was fair, from a financial point of view, to such holders, as more fully described in the section titled “The Merger—Opinion of Kraton’s Financial Advisor” below. Following discussion and thorough review, including discussion of the factors summarized in the section titled “The Merger—Reasons for the Merger” below, the Board unanimously determined that the entry into the Merger Agreement was the best potential strategic alternative available to Kraton and in the best interest of the stockholders of Kraton, including relative to the other strategic alternatives reviewed by the Board. The Board then declared advisable, adopted and approved the Merger Agreement, and recommended it to the Company’s stockholders for adoption.

On the morning of September 27, 2021, prior to the opening of regular way trading on the NYSE, Kraton, Parent, Merger Subsidiary and Intermediate Merger Subsidiary entered into the Merger Agreement and Kraton and Parent issued press releases announcing execution of the Merger Agreement.

Reasons for the Merger

In evaluating the Merger Agreement and the transactions contemplated thereby, including the Merger, the Board consulted with Kraton’s senior management, King & Spalding LLP and J.P. Morgan.

In the course of reaching its determination to approve the Merger Agreement and the transactions contemplated thereby, including the Merger, and to recommend that Kraton’s stockholders vote to approve the Merger Proposal, the Board considered a number of factors and benefits of the Merger, including the following factors weighing in favor of approving the Merger Agreement:

 

  ●  

Premium to Market Prices: The fact that the $46.50 price to be paid for each share of Kraton common stock represents a significant premium to recent and historical market prices of Kraton common stock, including a premium of approximately:

 

  ●  

46.9% to the $31.65 closing price on July 2, 2021, the last trading day prior to the publication of the Reuters report stating that Kraton was exploring a potential sale of Kraton; and

 

  ●  

39.4% to the $33.35 volume weighted average price for the 30-day period prior to the publication of the Reuters report.

 

  ●  

Cash Consideration: The fact that the Merger Consideration consists solely of cash, providing Kraton’s stockholders with certainty of value and liquidity upon consummation of the Merger.

 

  ●  

The Company’s Operating and Financial Condition. The Board’s consideration of its knowledge and familiarity with Kraton’s business, including its current and historical financial condition and results of operations, competitive position, properties and assets, as well as Kraton’s business strategy and prospects.

 

  ●  

Prospects of Kraton as an Independent Company. The Board’s evaluation of Kraton’s long-term strategic plan and the related execution risks and uncertainties (including the risk factors set forth in Kraton’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2020), and its weighing of the prospects of achieving long-term value for its stockholders through execution of Kraton’s strategic business plan against the value

 

41

Table of Contents
 

to stockholders that could be realized through the Merger at a significant premium to the recent and historical market prices of Kraton common stock.

 

  ●  

Review of Strategic Alternatives: The Board’s extended consideration of strategic alternatives, including, among others, remaining an independent company and pursuing Kraton’s strategic plan, executing on Kraton’s corporate development plan to enhance the existing polymer business, pursuing a Sum of the Parts Strategy, the sale of Kraton’s CST business, or pursuing a strategic transaction with, or the sale of Kraton to, another party (including those that submitted indications of interest prior to the execution of the Merger Agreement), and the Board’s belief, after a review of the proposals and discussions with Kraton’s management and advisors, that the value offered to stockholders in the Merger, combined with their assessment concerning the certainty of closing, was more favorable to the stockholders of Kraton than the potential value that might have resulted from other strategic opportunities reasonably available to Kraton.

 

  ●  

Likelihood of Completion. The Board’s belief that the Merger is likely to be completed, based on, among other things, the absence of a financing condition, the financial strength of Parent and Goldman Sachs Bank USA, which provided the Debt Commitment Letter, and the terms of the Debt Commitment Letter, the limited number of conditions to the Merger, and the likelihood of obtaining required regulatory approvals for the Merger and the terms of the Merger Agreement regarding the obligations of both companies to pursue such approvals.

 

  ●  

Kraton’s Remedies. The fact that if Parent does not consummate the Merger due to Parent’s failure to obtain its requisite Debt Financing, Kraton would be entitled to receive a reverse termination fee of $63 million, subject to the terms set forth in the Merger Agreement.

 

  ●  

Sale Process. The competitive nature of the sales process conducted by Kraton, together with its financial and legal advisors, in soliciting and evaluating multiple acquisition proposals for Kraton, and the number and terms of, and pricing set forth in, the acquisition proposals received by Kraton, and the Board’s determination that Parent’s proposal represented the best value and likelihood of closing reasonably available to Kraton’s stockholders.

 

  ●  

Advisors. The fact that Kraton’s legal and financial advisors were involved throughout the process and negotiations and updated the Board directly and regularly, which provided the Board with additional perspectives on the negotiations in addition to those of Kraton’s management.

 

  ●  

Negotiations with Parent: The course of discussions and negotiations between Kraton and Parent, improvements to the terms of Parent’s acquisition proposal in connection with those negotiations, including those ultimately resulting in Parent’s final price of $46.50 in cash per share of Kraton common stock, and the Board’s belief based on these negotiations, that Parent’s proposal represented the highest price per share of Kraton common stock that Parent was willing to pay and that these were the most favorable terms to Kraton to which Parent was willing to agree.

 

  ●  

Opinion of J.P. Morgan: The opinion of J.P. Morgan delivered orally to the Board on September 26, 2021, confirmed by delivery of a written opinion, dated September 27, 2021, to the effect that, as of such date and based upon and subject to the assumptions

 

42

Table of Contents
 

made, procedures followed, matters considered, and limitations on the review undertaken by J.P. Morgan in preparing its opinion, the Merger Consideration to be paid to the holders of Kraton common stock in the Merger was fair, from a financial point of view, to such holders, as more fully described in the section titled “The Merger—Opinion of Kraton’s Financial Advisor” below. The full text of the written opinion of J.P. Morgan, dated September 27, 2021, which sets forth, among other things, the assumptions made, procedures followed, matters considered and limitations on the review undertaken by J.P. Morgan in preparing its opinion, is attached as Annex B to this proxy statement and is incorporated herein by reference.

 

  ●  

Unanimous Board Determination. The fact that Board was unanimous in its determination to recommend that Kraton’s stockholders approve and adopt the Merger Agreement and the transactions contemplated thereby, including the Merger.

 

  ●  

Ability to Change Recommendation or Accept Superior Proposal. The Board’s ability under the Merger Agreement to withdraw or modify its recommendation in favor of the Merger under certain circumstances, and the Board’s ability to terminate the Merger Agreement in connection with a Superior Proposal (as specified in the Merger Agreement), subject to payment of a termination fee of $63 million, and the Board’s determination that the termination fee is within the customary range of termination fees for transactions of this type and is reasonable.

 

  ●  

Stockholder Vote: The fact that the Merger Agreement will be subject to approval and adoption by the affirmative vote of the holders of a majority of the outstanding shares of Kraton common stock entitled to vote thereon at the Special Meeting, and the absence of any commitments requiring any Kraton stockholders to vote in favor of the Merger Proposal at the Special Meeting, will allow Kraton’s stockholders to decide whether to approve the Merger Proposal.

The Board also considered a variety of risks and other potentially negative factors concerning the Merger and the Merger Agreement, including the following:

 

  ●  

No Stockholder Participation in Future Growth or Earnings: The nature of the transaction as an all-cash transaction prevents stockholders from being able to participate in any future earnings or growth of Kraton or Parent, and Kraton’s stockholders will not benefit from any potential future appreciation in the value of Kraton common stock, including any value that could be achieved if Kraton or Parent engages in future strategic or other transactions or as a result of the growth of Kraton’s or Parent’s operations.

 

  ●  

Effect of Failure to Complete the Merger: While the Board expects that the Merger will be completed, there can be no assurance that the required stockholder approval will be obtained or that all of the conditions to the completion of the Merger will be satisfied or waived or that the Merger will receive required regulatory approvals, and, as a result, it is possible that factors outside the control of Kraton or Parent could result in the Merger being completed at a later time, or not being completed at all, even if the Merger Proposal is approved by Kraton’s stockholders. The Board also considered potential negative effects if the Merger was not completed, including that:

 

  ●  

the trading price of Kraton common stock could be adversely affected;

 

  ●  

Kraton would have incurred significant transaction and opportunity costs attempting to complete the Merger, including the loss of potential acquisitions;

 

43

Table of Contents
  ●  

Kraton could lose business partners and employees after the announcement of the execution of the Merger Agreement;

 

  ●  

Kraton’s business may be subject to significant disruption;

 

  ●  

the market’s perceptions of Kraton’s prospects could be adversely affected; and

 

  ●  

Kraton’s directors, officers, and other employees would have expended considerable time and effort to negotiate, implement and complete the Merger, and their time may have been diverted from other important business opportunities and operational matters while working to implement the Merger.

 

  ●  

Flexibility to Operate the Business: The restrictions imposed by the Merger Agreement on the conduct of its business prior to the completion of the Merger, which require Kraton to operate the business only in the ordinary course of business and, generally, consistent with past practice, and that subject the operations of the business to other restrictions, which could delay or prevent Kraton from undertaking business opportunities, including the acquisition of businesses and entering into certain material contracts, that may arise prior to the completion of the Merger and that may have an adverse effect on Kraton’s ability to respond to changing market and business conditions in a timely manner or at all.

 

  ●  

Restrictions on Soliciting Proposals; Termination Fee. The restrictions in the Merger Agreement on the active solicitation of competing proposals and the requirement, under the Merger Agreement, that Kraton pay, if the Merger Agreement is terminated in certain circumstances, a termination fee of $63 million, which fee may deter third parties from making a competing offer for Kraton prior to the consummation of the Merger.

 

  ●  

Taxable Merger Consideration: The fact that the receipt of the Merger Consideration by Kraton’s stockholders will be fully taxable.

 

  ●  

Interests of the Board and Management: The directors and executive officers may have interests in the transactions contemplated by the Merger Agreement described in the section titled “The Merger—Interests of Certain Persons in the Merger” below that would be different from, or in addition to, those of Kraton’s stockholders.

The foregoing discussion of the factors considered by the Board is not intended to be exhaustive but does set forth the principal factors considered by the Board. The Board collectively reached the unanimous conclusion to approve the Merger and the Merger Agreement considering all of the various factors described above and other factors that each member of the Board deemed relevant. In view of the wide variety of factors considered by the members of the Board in connection with their evaluation of the Merger and the complexity of these matters, the Board did not consider it practical, and did not attempt, to quantify, rank or otherwise assign relative weights to the specific factors it considered in reaching its decision. The Board made its decision based on the totality of information presented to and considered by it. In considering the factors discussed above, individual directors may have given different weights to different factors.

In accordance with customary investment banking practice, J.P. Morgan employed generally accepted valuation methodologies in rendering its oral opinion to the Board on September 26, 2021, which was confirmed by delivery of a written opinion, dated September 27, 2021, and in the financial analyses presented to the Board on September 26, 2021 in connection with the rendering of such opinion. The following is a summary of the material financial analyses utilized by J.P. Morgan in connection with rendering its opinion to the Board and does not purport to be a complete description of the analyses or data presented by J.P. Morgan. Some of the summaries of the financial analyses include information presented in tabular format. The tables are not intended to stand alone, and in order to more fully understand the financial analyses used by J.P. Morgan, the tables must be read together with the full text of each summary. Discounted Cash Flow Analysis. J.P. Morgan conducted a discounted cash flow analysis with respect to each of the Case A, Case B, Case C and Case D Projections for the purpose of determining an implied fully diluted equity value per share for the Kraton common stock under each such case. J.P. Morgan calculated the unlevered free cash flows that Kraton is expected to generate during fiscal years 2021E through 2025E based upon each of the Case A, Case B, Case C and Case D Projections (as set forth in the section titled “The Merger—Management Projections” below, which was discussed with, and approved by, the Board for use by J.P. Morgan in connection with its financial analyses). J.P. Morgan also calculated a range of terminal values for Kraton at the end of this period under each of the Case A, Case B, Case C and Case D Projections by applying perpetual growth rates ranging from 1.5% to 2.5% to estimates of terminal revenue under each of the Case A, Case B, Case C and Case D Projections for Kraton at the end of fiscal-year 2025E, as provided in Kraton management projections under the applicable case. J.P. Morgan then discounted the unlevered free cash flow estimates and the range of terminal values to present value as of June 30, 2021 using discount rates ranging from 9.25% to 10.25% for the projected cash flows under each of the Case A, Case B, Case C and Case D Projections, except that discount rates ranging from 15.25% to 17.25% were used for the incremental projected cash flows for the breakthrough technologies included in each of the Case C and Case D Projections and the specialty polymer expansion project in Taiwan included in the Case D Projections. The discount rate ranges were chosen by J.P. Morgan based upon an analysis of the weighted average cost of capital of Kraton. The present value of the unlevered free cash flow estimates and the range of terminal values were then adjusted by subtracting net debt and other adjustments for Kraton as of June 30, 2021.

J.P. Morgan was selected to advise Kraton with respect to the Merger and deliver an opinion to the Board with respect to the Merger on the basis of, among other things, such experience and its qualifications and reputation in connection with such matters and its familiarity with Kraton and the industries in which it operates.

For financial advisory services rendered in connection with the Merger, Kraton has agreed to pay J.P. Morgan an estimated fee of approximately $32 million, $3.0 million of which became payable to J.P. Morgan at the time J.P. Morgan delivered its opinion and the remainder of which is contingent and payable upon the consummation of the Merger. In addition, Kraton has agreed to reimburse J.P. Morgan for its reasonable costs and expenses incurred in connection with its services, including the reasonable fees and expenses of counsel, and will indemnify J.P. Morgan against certain liabilities arising out of J.P. Morgan’s engagement. During the two years preceding the date of J.P. Morgan’s opinion, J.P. Morgan and its affiliates have had commercial or investment banking relationships with Kraton, for which J.P. Morgan and such affiliates have earned customary compensation. Such services during such period have included acting as joint lead bookrunner on Kraton’s offering of debt securities in December 2020 and as financial advisor to Kraton on its sale of its Cariflex business in March 2020. During the two years preceding the date of this proxy statement, neither J.P. Morgan nor its affiliates have had any material financial advisory or other material commercial or investment banking relationships with Parent or with DL Holdings Co., Ltd., the parent company of Parent. In addition, J.P. Morgan and its affiliates hold, on a proprietary basis, less than 1% of the outstanding Kraton common stock and common stock of DL Holdings Co., Ltd. During the two-year period preceding delivery of its opinion ending on September 27, 2021, the aggregate fees recognized by J.P. Morgan from Kraton were approximately $10 million. In the ordinary course of their businesses, J.P. Morgan and its affiliates may actively trade the debt and equity securities or financial instruments (including derivatives, bank loans or other obligations) of Kraton or the Parent for their own account or for the accounts of customers and, accordingly, they may at any time hold long or short positions in such securities or other financial instruments.

Management Projections

In connection with the evaluation of Kraton’s strategic alternatives described in this proxy statement, Kraton’s management prepared and provided certain non-public, unaudited prospective financial information to the Board in considering, analyzing and evaluating Kraton’s strategic alternatives, including the Merger, and to Kraton’s financial advisor, J.P. Morgan for its use and reliance in connection with J.P. Morgan’s financial analyses and opinion described in the section titled “The Merger—Opinion of Kraton’s Financial Advisor” above. This unaudited prospective financial information (“Management Projections”) consisted of forecasts under four different scenarios, the Case A Projections, the Case B Projections, the Case C Projections and the Case D Projections, as detailed below.

Kraton’s management directed J.P. Morgan to use and rely upon the Case A Projections, the Case B Projections, the Case C Projections and the Case D Projections, and to view each case independently, for purposes of J.P. Morgan’s discounted cash flow analysis and such use was approved by the Board. Kraton’s management also directed J.P. Morgan to use and rely upon the Case C Projections for purposes of J.P. Morgan’s public trading multiples analysis and selected transaction analysis and such use was approved by the Board.

Morgan or the Board for purposes of their respective evaluations. Accordingly, we have not provided a reconciliation of the financial measures included in Management Projections to the relevant GAAP financial measures.

Kraton also believes that a quantitative reconciliation of such forward-looking information to the most comparable financial measure calculated and presented in accordance with GAAP cannot be made available without unreasonable efforts. A reconciliation of forward-looking non-GAAP financial measures would require Kraton to quantify stock-based compensation expense, acquisition and integration expense, amortization expense associated with acquired intangibles, asset impairment charges, restructuring charges, gains or losses relating to sales of assets, tax-related items and the non-cash portion of the interest expense on Kraton’s existing debt. All of these items cannot be reliably quantified due to the combination of variability and volatility of such components and may, depending on the size of the components, have a significant impact on the reconciliation.

Furthermore, our independent registered public accounting firm, has not examined, reviewed, compiled or otherwise applied procedures to the Management Projections and, accordingly, assumes no responsibility for, and expresses no opinion on, the Management Forecasts. Many of these estimates and assumptions are difficult to predict, subject to significant economic and competitive uncertainties, are beyond our control, and may cause Management Projections or the underlying assumptions to be inaccurate. Since Management Projections cover multiple years, the information contained therein, and the estimates and assumptions on which such forecasts are based, by their nature become even less reliable with each successive year. Overview of Management Projections

The cases of Management Projections described herein were prepared by Kraton management based on various estimated cash flows reflecting four different progressive and future opportunities built on a common underlying base case (Case A Projections), as follows:

 

  ●  

Case A Projections: The Case A Projections reflect Kraton’s management’s forecasted financial performance of Kraton’s chemical and polymer segments through 2025. The Case A Projections exclude non-cash EBITDA contributions arising under Kraton’s Isoprene Rubber Supply Agreement (which we refer to as the “IRSA”). The IRSA is a multi-year agreement that Kraton entered into in 2020 in connection with the sale of its Cariflex business to Daelim Industrial Co, Ltd. whereby Kraton agreed to supply isoprene rubber at cost to Daelim Industrial Co, Ltd. for a period of five years, with an optional extension for an additional five years.

 

  ●  

Case B Projections: The Case B Projections were based on the same assumptions as the Case A Projections, except that the Case B Projections include long-term non-cash EBITDA arising under the IRSA, and assume that Kraton will be able to convert such value to cash.

 

  ●  

Case C Projections: The Case C Projections were based on the same assumptions as the Case B Projections, except that the Case C Projections include EBITDA achieved by 2025 based on the success of certain “breakthrough technologies” of Kraton, which consist of products and technologies in Kraton’s innovation portfolio that have been or are in the early stages of being brought to market.

 

  ●  

Case D Projections: The Case D Projections were based on the same assumptions as the Case C Projections, except that the Case D Projections include EBITDA realizable from Kraton’s specialty polymer expansion project in Taiwan.

Certain Definitions:

 

  ●  

“EBITDA (including IRSA)” means earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, and includes isoprene rubber sales under the IRSA.

 

  ●  

“EBITDA (excluding IRSA)” means earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, and does not include isoprene rubber sales under the IRSA.

 

  ●  

“Unlevered Free Cash Flows” means net operating profit after taxes, plus depreciation and amortization, less capital expenditures, less working capital.

Financing of the Merger

We anticipate that the total amount of funds necessary for Parent to complete the Merger and the related transactions, and to pay the fees and expenses required to be paid at the closing of the

 

55

Table of Contents

Merger by Parent and Merger Subsidiary under the Merger Agreement, will be approximately $2.5 billion, which will be funded by a portion of the proceeds of the Debt Financing, together with available cash of Parent. This amount includes the funds needed to: (1) pay Kraton stockholders the amounts due under the Merger Agreement, (2) to refinance certain outstanding debt of Kraton and its subsidiaries and (3) make payments in respect of our outstanding equity-based awards (including Options and Company RSUs) pursuant to the Merger Agreement.

In connection with the Merger Agreement, Parent entered into the Debt Commitment Letter with the Debt Commitment Party pursuant to which the Debt Commitment Party has committed to provide, upon certain terms and subject to certain conditions, Parent with certain Debt Financing in aggregate principal amount of up to $1.75 billion. A portion of the proceeds of the Debt Financing will be used to fund the Merger and related transactions, and to pay related fees and expenses required to be paid by Parent under the Merger Agreement. In addition, the proceeds under the Debt Financing will be used (1) to provide ongoing working capital, and (2) for other general corporate purposes.

The Merger Agreement does not contain a financing condition. For more information, see the sections titled “The Merger Agreement—Conditions to Completion of the Merger” and “The Merger—Termination Fee; Effect of Termination” below.

Closing and Effective Time of the Merger

The closing of the Merger will occur by means of the exchange of signatures electronically at 7:00 a.m. Houston, Texas time, as soon as possible, but in any event no later than two business days following the date the conditions set forth in the Merger Agreement (other than those conditions that by their nature are to be satisfied or waived at the closing, but subject to the satisfaction or waiver of those conditions at the closing) have been satisfied or, to the extent permissible, waived, or on such other time or on such other date as Kraton and Parent may mutually agree unless the marketing period to syndicate participation in the Debt Financing prior to the closing date in accordance with the Debt Commitment Letter has not ended, in which case the closing will instead occur on the earlier of (1) a date during the marketing period specified by Parent on not less than two business days’ written notice to Kraton and (2) the last day of the marketing period.

On the closing date, Kraton and Parent will cause a certificate of merger relating to the Merger to be executed and filed with the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware as provided in Section 251 of the DGCL. The Merger will become effective at such time of the filing of the certificate of merger, or at such later time that Kraton and Parent may agree and designate in the certificate of merger in accordance with Delaware law.

Payment of Merger Consideration and Surrender of Stock Certificates

Promptly after the effective time of the Merger (but in no event later than three business days after the effective time), each holder of record of a certificate representing shares of Kraton common stock (other than holders who solely hold excluded shares) will be sent a letter of transmittal and instructions describing how such record holder may surrender his, her or its shares of our common stock (or affidavits of loss in lieu thereof) in exchange for the per share Merger Consideration.

Litigation Related to the Merger

As of November 3, 2021, three lawsuits have been filed on behalf of individuals purporting to be Kraton stockholders challenging certain public disclosures concerning the Merger. The first complaint was filed on October 21, 2021 in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and is styled Ryan O’Dell v. Kraton Corporation, et al., Case No. 1:21-cv-08642. The second complaint was filed on October 28, 2021 in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and is styled Ciccotelli v. Kraton Corporation, et al., Case No. 1:21-cv-08802. The third complaint was filed on November 1, 2021 in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and is styled Shumacher v. Kraton Corporation, et al., Case No. 1:21-cv-08922. Each of the Stockholder Actions names Kraton and the members of its Board as defendants.

The Stockholder Actions purport to allege claims for violations of Sections 14(a) and 20(a) of the Exchange Act and Rule 14a-9 promulgated under the Exchange Act. The O’Dell complaint also alleges violations of 17 C.F.R. § 244.100. The plaintiffs in the Stockholder Actions generally allege that the proxy disclosures related to the Merger omit material information relating to (i) certain non-GAAP financial metrics included in projections set forth in the proxy statement and (ii) certain

 

59

Table of Contents

analyses prepared by J.P. Morgan in connection with the Board’s evaluation of the Merger, and that the omission of such information renders the proxy disclosures false and misleading. The plaintiffs in the Stockholder Actions seek, among other things, an injunction preventing the consummation of the Merger, or, if the Merger is consummated, rescission of the Merger or an award of rescissory or other damages, a declaration that the defendants violated Sections 14(a) and 20(a) of the Exchange Act and Rule 14a-9, and an award of the costs of the action, including attorneys’ and experts’ fees.

Kraton believes the Stockholder Actions are without merit and vigorously denies that it has committed any violation of law or duties or engaged in any alleged wrongful conduct. Kraton cannot predict the outcome of or estimate the possible loss or range of loss, if any, from the aforementioned matters. Additional complaints may be filed in connection with the Merger, which could prevent or delay completion of the Merger and result in substantial costs to Kraton. If additional similar complaints or demands are filed or made, absent new or different allegations that are material, Kraton will not necessarily announce them.

Material U.S. Federal Income Tax Consequences of the Merger

The following is a discussion of the material U.S. federal income tax consequences of the Merger to holders of our common stock whose shares are exchanged for cash pursuant to the Merger. This discussion is based on the provisions of the Internal Revenue Code (the “Code”), applicable U.S. Treasury regulations (“Treasury Regulations”), judicial authorities, and administrative interpretations, each as in effect as of the date of this proxy statement. These authorities are subject to change, possibly on a retroactive basis, and any such change could affect the accuracy of the statements and conclusions set forth in this discussion. We cannot assure you that the Internal Revenue Service (the “IRS”) will not challenge one or more of the tax consequences described in this discussion or that a court would not sustain such challenge.

This discussion applies only to holders of shares of Kraton common stock who hold such shares as a “capital asset” within the meaning of Section 1221 of the Code (generally, property held for investment). Further, this discussion does not purport to consider all aspects of U.S. federal income taxation that may be relevant to a holder in light of such holder’s particular circumstances, or that may apply to a holder that is subject to special treatment under the U.S. federal income tax laws (including, for example, insurance companies, dealers or brokers in securities or foreign currencies, traders in securities who elect the mark-to-market method of accounting, holders that have a functional currency other than the U.S. dollar, persons who are required to recognize income or gain with respect to the Merger no later than such income or gain is required to be reported on an applicable financial statement, tax-exempt organizations, retirement plans, individual retirement accounts or other tax-deferred or advantaged accounts (or persons holding Kraton common stock through such plans or accounts), cooperatives, banks and certain other financial institutions, real estate investment trusts, regulated investment companies, certain former citizens or former long-term residents of the United States, “controlled foreign corporations,” “passive foreign investment companies,” “qualified foreign pension funds” (within the meaning of section 897(l)(2) of the Code) or entities all of the interests in which are held by a qualified foreign pension fund, partnerships (including entities or arrangements classified as partnerships for U.S. federal income tax purposes), S corporations, or other pass-through entities or investors in partnerships (including entities or arrangements classified as partnerships for U.S. federal income tax purposes) or such other entities, holders who hold shares of Kraton common stock as part of a hedge, straddle, constructive sale, conversion or other integrated or risk reduction transaction, holders of more than 5% of the shares of Kraton common stock, holders who acquired their shares of Kraton common stock

 

60

Table of Contents

through the exercise of employee stock options or other compensation arrangements and holders of dissenting shares). Moreover, this discussion does not address the tax consequences of the Merger arising under any applicable state, local, or foreign tax laws or the application of other U.S. federal taxes, such as the federal estate tax, the federal gift tax, the “Medicare” tax on certain net investment income, the alternative minimum tax, or any withholding considerations under FATCA (defined for this purpose as sections 1471 through 1474 of the Code, the Treasury Regulations and administrative guidance thereunder and the intergovernmental agreements entered into, and laws and regulations promulgated, pursuant thereto or in connection therewith).

If a partnership (including for this purpose any entity or arrangement treated as a partnership for U.S. federal income tax purposes) holds shares of Kraton common stock, the tax treatment of a partner in such partnership will generally depend on the status of the partners and the activities of the partnership. If you are a partner of a partnership holding shares of Kraton common stock, you should consult your tax advisor.

For purposes of this discussion, the term “U.S. Holder” means a beneficial owner of common stock that is for U.S. federal income tax purposes:

 

  ●  

a citizen or individual resident of the United States;

 

  ●  

a corporation, or other entity taxable as a corporation for U.S. federal income tax purposes, created or organized in or under the laws of the United States, any state thereof, or the District of Columbia;

 

  ●  

a trust if (1) a court within the United States is able to exercise primary supervision over the trust’s administration and one or more U.S. persons are authorized to control all substantial decisions of the trust, or (2) the trust has a valid election in effect under applicable Treasury Regulations to be treated as a U.S. person; or

 

  ●  

an estate, the income of which is subject to U.S. federal income tax regardless of its source.

For purposes of this discussion, a “non-U.S. Holder” is a beneficial owner of common stock, other than an entity or arrangement classified as a partnership for U.S. federal income tax purposes, that is not a U.S. Holder.

Holders of Kraton common stock are urged to consult their own tax advisors regarding the application of the U.S. federal tax laws to their particular situation and the applicability and effect of state, local or foreign tax laws and tax treaties.

Consequences to U.S. Holders

The receipt of cash by U.S. Holders in exchange for shares of Kraton common stock pursuant to the Merger will be a taxable transaction for U.S. federal income tax purposes. In general, a U.S. Holder who receives cash in exchange for shares of Kraton common stock pursuant to the Merger will recognize gain or loss in an amount equal to the difference, if any, between (1) the amount of cash received and (2) the U.S. Holder’s adjusted tax basis in such shares of Kraton common stock. A U.S. Holder’s adjusted tax basis will generally equal the price the U.S. Holder paid for such share.

Any such gain or loss recognized by a U.S. Holder upon the exchange of shares of Kraton common stock pursuant to the Merger generally will be capital gain or loss and will be long-term capital gain or loss if the U.S. Holder’s holding period in its shares of Kraton common stock is more than one year on the closing date of the Merger. Long-term capital gains of non-corporate U.S. Holders generally are eligible for preferential U.S. federal income tax rates under current law. The deductibility of capital

 

61

Table of Contents

losses is subject to limitations. If a U.S. Holder acquired different blocks of Kraton common stock at different times and different prices, such U.S. Holder must determine its adjusted tax basis and holding period separately with respect to each block of Kraton common stock.

Consequences to Non-U.S. Holders

Subject to the discussion below in “The Merger—Material U.S. Federal Income Tax Consequences of the Merger—Information Reporting and Backup Withholding,” a non-U.S. Holder who receives cash in exchange for its shares of Kraton common stock in the Merger generally will not be subject to U.S. federal income tax on gain recognized on such exchange unless:

 

  ●  

such gain is effectively connected with the non-U.S. Holder’s conduct of a U.S. trade or business (and, if required by an applicable treaty, is attributable to a permanent establishment or fixed base maintained by the non-U.S. Holder in the United States);

 

  ●  

the non-U.S. Holder is an individual who is present in the United States for 183 days or more in the taxable year in which the Merger occurs and certain other conditions are satisfied; or

 

  ●  

the non-U.S. Holder’s Kraton common stock constitutes a “United States real property interest” as defined in the Code (a “USRPI”).

A non-U.S. Holder described in the first bullet above generally will be subject to U.S. federal income tax in the same manner as a U.S. Holder with respect to the receipt of cash in exchange for Kraton common stock in the Merger. A non-U.S. Holder that is a corporation may also be subject to an additional “branch profits tax” at a rate of 30% (or such lower rate as may be specified by an applicable treaty) on its effectively connected earnings and profits for the taxable year, subject to certain adjustments.

Gain recognized with respect to shares of Kraton common stock surrendered in the Merger by a non-U.S. Holder who is described in the second bullet above generally will be subject to U.S. federal income tax at a 30% rate (or such lower rate as may be specified by an applicable treaty) but may be offset by certain U.S. source capital losses, if any, of the non-U.S. Holder.

With respect to the third bullet above, the non-U.S. Holder’s Kraton common stock will not be treated as a USRPI unless Kraton is or has been a “United States real property holding corporation,” as defined in the Code (a “USRPHC”), at any time during the five-year period ending on the date of the Merger or the non-U.S. Holder’s holding period, whichever period is shorter. We do not believe that we have been or will become a USRPHC at any time during the five-year period ending on the date of the Merger. Further, even if contrary to our expectation, Kraton were treated as a USRPHC at any time during the applicable period, the non-U.S. Holder’s Kraton common stock will not be treated as a USRPI unless (1) our common stock was not regularly traded on an established securities market (within the meaning of Section 1.897-9T(d) of the Treasury Regulations) prior to the Merger, or (2) such holder owned, actually or constructively, more than 5% of our common stock during the applicable period described above. If a non-U.S. Holder’s Kraton common stock constitutes a USRPI, such non-U.S. Holder will be subject to U.S. federal income tax on the gain recognized in the Merger on a net basis in the same manner as a U.S. Holder and withholding may apply.

Information Reporting and Backup Withholding

Payments made in exchange for shares of Kraton common stock pursuant to the Merger may be subject, under certain circumstances, to information reporting and backup withholding (currently at a rate of 24%). To avoid backup withholding, a U.S. Holder that does not otherwise establish an

 

62

Table of Contents

exemption should complete and return IRS Form W-9, certifying that such U.S. Holder is a U.S. person, the taxpayer identification number provided is correct, and such U.S. Holder is not subject to backup withholding. In general, a non-U.S. Holder will not be subject to backup withholding with respect to cash payments to the non-U.S. Holder pursuant to the Merger if the non-U.S. Holder has provided an applicable IRS Form W-8. Backup withholding is not an additional tax. Any amounts withheld under the backup withholding rules may be refunded or credited against a holder’s U.S. federal income tax liability, if any, provided that such holder furnishes the required information to the IRS in a timely manner.

This summary of the material U.S. federal income tax consequences of the Merger is for general information purposes only and is not tax advice. Holders of Kraton common stock should consult their own tax advisors regarding the application of the U.S. federal tax laws to their particular situation and the applicability and effect of state, local or foreign tax laws and tax treaties.
